clue.text: How to begin to spell Assyrian ancient capital

indicators.note: beginning to spell a word means saying its opening letters one by one, in order

parts.note: the first letter of the word
how you spell it is a sequence, this letter followed by the next, and the word for 'followed by' joins them
the second letter of the word

explanation.surface: A note on how to write the name of an old Assyrian capital such as Nineveh.
explanation.walkthrough: Begin spelling Assyrian and you say 'A, THEN S': the word THEN that joins the two letters is part of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Athens was the leading city-state of classical Greece and remains the Greek capital today.

clue.text: Picked Yorkshire's best batsman, settled in

parts.note: picked, as in chose or selected
Joe Root, the Yorkshire and England batter, often called England's best

explanation.surface: A cricket selector chose the top Yorkshire batsman, who then made himself at home in the side.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe Root is a Yorkshire cricketer and England's leading Test run-scorer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant that has grown roots has established itself, and figuratively anything that has become firmly established in a place.

clue.text: All European, so united

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for European
so, as in 'so good' meaning very good
people united are as one

explanation.surface: A statement that all Europeans are thereby joined together.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun meaning every person, used just as 'all' is in 'all were present'.

clue.text: Key moments in court proceedings, job of signalman?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: on a tennis court, the points that can win a set
second meaning: a railway signalman switches tracks by setting the points

explanation.surface: Crucial stages of a legal trial, and the work of a railway signalman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court, but it is a tennis court. On British railways, points are the movable rails that switch a train between tracks.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis a player one point from winning a set has set points; a signalman literally adjusts the railway switches.

clue.text: Mum punches vulgar knight, an awful bully

indicators.note: to punch is to drive a hole into something, so this word is pushed into the middle of what follows

parts.note: flash means showy and tasteless
an informal word for mother
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A mother lands a blow on a coarse knight, a dreadful bully.
explanation.walkthrough: Flashman is the bully in Thomas Hughes's Victorian school novel Tom Brown's School Days.
explanation.definitionFit: Harry Flashman torments the younger boys at Rugby School in that Victorian novel, the archetypal schoolboy tormentor.

clue.text: Leave by plane … its name? "Go Ballistic"

parts.note: to depart by air
'its' points to the plane, so the article stands in
handle is slang for a name, as in a CB radio handle

explanation.surface: A departing flight whose name, in quotation marks, is 'Go Ballistic'.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks and capitals are surface dressing; the quoted phrase is simply the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to lose one's temper suddenly, just as going ballistic does.

clue.text: Son, mischievous, inconsiderate

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for son
like an elf, impish and full of pranks

explanation.surface: A description of a naughty, thoughtless boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who thinks only of themselves is lacking in thought for other people.

clue.text: Pacino: men massively upset suppressing reminder

indicators.note: upset means turned over, and in a down entry that reads the letters from the bottom up
to suppress something is to keep it out of sight, so the words conceal a run of letters

parts.note: the letters run consecutively from inside the actor's name to the start of the last word, ignoring the colon

explanation.surface: Al Pacino and his co-stars are greatly upset, holding back something meant to jog the memory.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes it look like an anagram of Pacino and men; the answer simply lies backwards across three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhyme or phrase that helps you recall something, such as a list or a spelling, is a memory aid.

clue.text: North American travel industry striking over practice denying coverage

parts.note: N for North and A for American

indicators.note: striking out means crossing off, so something is removed from the industry word

parts.note: the business of holidays and travel
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: An American travel firm on strike over a policy refusing insurance cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coverage' suggests insurance, but here it means clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Nudism is the habit of going without clothes, so it refuses any covering of the body.

clue.text: Witches go bareback riding here, famously

parts.note: a gathering of witches
a go is an attempt

explanation.surface: Witches riding horses without saddles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bareback' really means naked: legend says Lady Godiva rode naked through Coventry, the English Midlands city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Godiva legend is set in that Midlands city, where she is said to have ridden unclothed through the streets.

clue.text: German prince's alarm, ringing bells at the front

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so the alarm word goes round the other piece

parts.note: an alert is a warning or alarm signal

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening, so only its leading letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A German prince's alarm clock rings its bells.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg was Queen Victoria's German-born husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert was a prince of the German duchy of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha before he married Victoria.

clue.text: Grand, flowery sprays, 22 Across in a pack

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for grand, a thousand pounds

indicators.note: a spray scatters things in all directions, so the letters before it are scattered

parts.note: taken as written, as the fodder

explanation.surface: Grand, flowery sprays of blossom, with a cross-reference to another answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 Across is ANIMAL; this one hunts in packs.
explanation.definitionFit: The grey wolf is the common wild wolf, a predator that lives and hunts in family packs.

clue.text: Strict exactitude chap fitting out ship discussed

indicators.note: something discussed is talked about, so the word is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: a rigger is the man who fits a ship with masts, ropes and sails

explanation.surface: A precise man rigging a ship, talked about.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the two words sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigour means severe precision and thoroughness, the quality of being exact and strict.

clue.text: Very small business of Conan the Barbaric?

indicators.note: barbaric means wild and uncivilised, so the letters are treated roughly and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as the fodder

explanation.surface: A question about Conan the Barbarian running a tiny business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barbaric' plays on Conan the Barbarian, the sword-wielding pulp hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Nanotechnology is engineering on the scale of billionths of a metre, so it is work on the very smallest things.

clue.text: Free baccy, rum, somewhere to go surfing?

indicators.note: rum in British slang means odd or peculiar, so the letters are made strange

parts.note: taken as written, as the fodder; baccy is British slang for tobacco

explanation.surface: An offer of free tobacco and rum at a seaside spot for surfers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' poses as the drink. The surfing is on the internet, not the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: An internet café is a place offering computers for browsing the web, which is surfing in the online sense.

clue.text: Seaport cleared out by you once, an eyesore

indicators.note: clearing out a word empties its middle, so only its outer letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
ye is an old form of you

explanation.surface: A port emptied by you long ago, a blot on the landscape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eyesore' looks like an ugly sight, but it is read literally: a sore on the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid, literally a sore spot on the eye.

clue.text: Discrete part

definitions.meaning: first meaning, an adjective: distinct, standing apart
second meaning, a verb: to divide or move apart

explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' looks like a noun, but here it is the verb, as in the waves parted.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means distinct and individual; the verb means to divide or come away from each other.

clue.text: A bit of spare time so Yank goes round national park

indicators.note: going round means turning to face the other way, so the letters are read backwards
a bit of the following words is a run of their letters, not the whole

parts.note: the letters run consecutively from the end of the first word into the last

explanation.surface: A spare moment lets an American tour a national park.
explanation.definitionFit: Yosemite in California's Sierra Nevada is one of the oldest and best-known protected parks in the United States.

clue.text: Fiddle starts to sound clearer after maintenance

indicators.note: the starts of the following words are their first letters

parts.note: the first letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A violin begins to sound clearer once it has been serviced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' poses as the violin; here it is the slang noun for a dishonest scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiddle in British slang is a swindle or fraud, the same as a con.

clue.text: Scottish plane tree said to be less healthy again

indicators.note: said means spoken out, so the words are heard rather than read

parts.note: less healthy is sicker, and again is more, as in once more

explanation.surface: A Scottish tree is reported to be ailing once more.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scotland the sycamore maple is commonly called the plane tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The sycamore is a maple with plane-like leaves, and Scots traditionally call it the plane.

clue.text: Bird in a duel changing height

indicators.note: in places the bird inside the jumbled letters of the other words
changing means altering, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as the fodder
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: A bird fighting a duel changes its height in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: Altitude is the elevation of something above sea level or the ground.

clue.text: Council skilfully collecting litter sent round

indicators.note: collecting means gathering up, so the adverb holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: doing something ably is doing it with skill

indicators.note: sent round means turned about, so the word for litter faces the other way

parts.note: litter strewn about makes a mess

explanation.surface: A local council deftly gathering up rubbish that has been scattered around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' looks like the definition's subject matter, but it only supplies the reversed letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An assembly is a gathered body of representatives that makes decisions, as a council does.

clue.text: Bill, adult chap, tense, unyielding

parts.note: an ad, a bill posted to advertise something
A is the old film-certificate abbreviation for adult
a chap is a man
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Bill, a grown man who is stressed and refuses to give way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name; it is a poster.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is resolute and will not be moved by persuasion is unbending, refusing to give in.

clue.text: Perhaps Greystoke title dad rejected?

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the combined letters are read backwards

parts.note: a title is the name of a book or film
an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A question about whether Lord Greystoke's inherited title was turned down by his father.
explanation.walkthrough: Greystoke is Tarzan's real identity, John Clayton, Lord Greystoke, raised by apes in Burroughs's stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarzan, heir to the Greystoke title, grew up among apes in the jungle and is the classic example of such a man.

clue.text: Mole unfinished, temperature 1 Celsius in the sea at Rimini

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its ending, so the last letter goes

parts.note: Adrian Mole, the teenage diarist of Sue Townsend's comic novels
T is the abbreviation for temperature
the Roman numeral for one
C is the abbreviation for Celsius

explanation.surface: A half-built breakwater, a thermometer reading of one degree, and the sea off an Italian resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mole' looks like a breakwater or a spy; it is Adrian Mole, the hero of a popular British comic diary series.
explanation.definitionFit: Rimini is a resort on Italy's east coast, which faces the Adriatic, the arm of the Mediterranean between Italy and the Balkans.

clue.text: Being uptight, this compiler's taken inside

indicators.note: taken inside means held within, so the compiler's words sit in the middle

parts.note: short for anal-retentive, fussy and tense
the setter speaking of himself: I'm, short for I am

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to being tense and to having been taken in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' poses as a verb but is the noun, a living creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A being is any living creature, and an animal is a living organism of that kind.

clue.text: Heard terrible record in conversation

indicators.note: heard means listened to, so the following words are taken by their sound

parts.note: terrible is dire, and a record is a log, such as a ship's log

explanation.surface: An awful recording is overheard during a chat.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the R of dire is not sounded.
explanation.definitionFit: Dialogue is spoken exchange between two or more people, the talk that makes up a discussion.

clue.text: Toothless former Tory PM, rubbish leader of Empire

parts.note: Anthony Eden, Conservative prime minister 1955-57
tat is cheap, tasteless rubbish

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A toothless ex-prime minister, dismissed as rubbish, who led the British Empire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toothless' suggests a feeble politician, but it is the literal zoological term.
explanation.definitionFit: Edentate is the zoological term for mammals such as anteaters and sloths that lack teeth or have very few.

clue.text: Leaders of English League, smooth football team?

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their first letters

parts.note: the first letter of each word
an even surface is smooth and level

explanation.surface: The teams heading the English football league are on a level footing.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: a football side has this many players.
explanation.definitionFit: A football team fields this number of players, so the side itself is often called by that number.
